source: Na, Grossmann, Varnum, Kitayama, Gonzalez & Nisbett (2010) Cultural differences are not always reducible to individual differences. PNAS 107(14):6192-6197
finding: Large study with 10 measures of independent vs interdependent social orientation and 10 measures of analytic vs holistic cognitive style. The measures separate groups (cultures, social classes) well. Inside groups the measures barely correlate with each other.
numbers: 10 social + 10 cognitive measures. Intercorrelations described as 'negligible'. Sample sizes and per-pair r not obtained: PMC full text was blocked (browser check) and Europe PMC returned HTTP 500. Only the abstract was read (via PubMed eutils). The task text calls this 'Na et al. 2009'; that is the unpublished manuscript cited by Varnum et al. 2010. The published version is 2010.
quote: behavioral constructs that distinguish among groups need not be valid as measures of individual differences
limits: Abstract only in this session. A poster version (APS 2011) lists 5 social and 11 cognitive measures, so the measure counts differ by version; the PNAS count is 10 + 10. Group means come from cultures and social classes; detail on which groups was not read.
agent_relevance: Core caution: a style that separates groups does not describe single cases. Do not assign a 'holistic' or 'analytic' style to one prompt or one run from group-level findings.

source: Varnum, Grossmann, Kitayama & Nisbett (2010) The origin of cultural differences in cognition: evidence for the social orientation hypothesis. Current Directions in Psychological Science 19(1):9-13
finding: Reports the individual-level result of Na et al.: a battery of social-orientation and cognitive-style tasks gave a very small correlation between a person's composite scores on the two domains, and almost no correlation among tasks inside each domain.
numbers: Composite social vs composite cognitive: r = .11. Mean correlation among tasks within each domain: r < .06.
quote: the two dimensions are very weak as individual differences
limits: Cites Na et al. as an unpublished 2009 manuscript. Review, not the primary data. Footnote 2: culture-level and individual-level structure do match for some constructs, for example the Big Five.
agent_relevance: Gives the headline numbers (r = .11, < .06). Shows that 'weak' means near zero for any single task as a predictor of another task.

source: Varnum et al. (2010) Current Directions in Psychological Science (same paper), explanation section
finding: The authors' account of why groups differ but individuals do not: independence or analytic thought may be expressed through different behaviours in different people, so single indicators correlate weakly while an aggregate still marks the group level. Example: one person is independent through a strong unique self, another through working alone.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Shweder (1973) 'The between and within of cross-cultural research'.
quote: There can be large differences between groups on a given dimension but only very weak individual differences within groups
limits: This is a post hoc explanation, stated as 'it would seem likely'. The paper itself lists as open: why the constructs cohere at group but not individual level.
agent_relevance: Group-level style is a profile averaged over many different routes. An agent should not treat one indicator (one task result) as a reliable sign of a style.

source: Varnum et al. (2010) Current Directions (same paper), caution on causality
finding: The authors admit that the missing match between individual and cultural level means a third variable could explain the covariation of social orientation and cognition. They list open questions: is the link one-way, why group level but not individual level.
numbers: None.
quote: some third variable may account for findings described throughout this review
limits: Written by the proponents of the social orientation hypothesis, so it is a self-reported limit.
agent_relevance: Even the theory's authors do not claim individual-level prediction. Our schema should not use cultural style labels as a cause of an agent's behaviour.

source: Varnum et al. (2010) Current Directions, within-culture comparisons list
finding: Group-level support comes from tight contrasts: Eastern vs Western Europe, Europe vs US, northern vs southern Italy, Hokkaido vs mainland Japan, adjacent Turkish villages, working vs middle class US. In each, the more interdependent group was also more holistic.
numbers: No effect sizes given in this review. Cited sources: Uskul et al. 2008 (farm/fish vs herding villages); Kitayama et al. 2006 (Hokkaido); Knight & Nisbett 2007 (Italy); Grossmann et al. 2009 (US class, unpublished).
limits: All of these are group comparisons, which is exactly the level where Na et al. found coherence. Several cited sources are unpublished manuscripts.
agent_relevance: The evidence base for the theory is group-mean differences only; it says nothing about how to predict one person.

source: Oyserman & Lee (2008) Does culture influence what and how we think? Effects of priming individualism and collectivism. Psychological Bulletin 134(2):311-342
finding: Meta-analysis of priming studies. Priming individualism or collectivism shifts cognition and relationality with moderate effects and self-concept and values with small effects. Effects are robust across prime types and in line with cross-national effects.
numbers: Abstract: moderate for relationality and cognition, small for self-concept and values. The mean d = .53 comes from the Varnum et al. 2010 review (read), which says prime types did not differ and Western and Asian samples gave comparable sizes.
limits: Abstract read only (PubMed). Mostly Western samples. Priming moves people inside a session, which is a within-person causal test, not an individual-differences test.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a context cue can move an individual, even if a person's trait score does not predict. Fits an agent design that sets framing by the task, not by an assumed style.

source: Oyserman, Coon & Kemmelmeier (2002) Rethinking individualism and collectivism. Psychological Bulletin 128(1):3-72
finding: Meta-analysis of individualism-collectivism differences. European Americans are more individualistic and less collectivistic than many groups, but not more individualistic than African Americans or Latinos, and not less collectivistic than Japanese or Koreans. Among Asians only Chinese show large effects.
numbers: Abstract: moderate effects on self-concept and relationality; large effects on attribution and cognitive style.
limits: Abstract only. Published with four commentaries in the same issue. Nation-level contrasts, not individual-level.
agent_relevance: The group-level story is itself uneven: the East-West contrast is not uniform even at group level, so it is weaker still for a single case.

source: Heine, Lehman, Peng & Greenholtz (2002) What's wrong with cross-cultural comparisons of subjective Likert scales? The reference-group effect. JPSP 82(6):903-918
finding: Self-report scales of collectivism failed to show the East-Asian vs North-American difference that cultural experts agree on. People rate themselves against different reference groups. Manipulating the reference group restored the expected differences.
numbers: Pilot + Study 1: trait and attitude measures failed to show the expected pattern. Study 3: groups from different cultural backgrounds in the same country differed more than people from different countries. Sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Competing explanation for weak individual-level links: the self-report measures themselves are biased by the comparison standard.
agent_relevance: For an LLM tested with a Likert self-report, the scale answers come from a reference standard, not from the thinking style. Prefer behavioural tasks over self-report.

source: Vignoles et al. (2016) Beyond the 'East-West' dichotomy: global variation in cultural models of selfhood. J Exp Psychol Gen 145(8):966-1000
finding: Common self-report measures of independence and interdependence often fail to show predicted cultural differences. The authors built and validated a 7-dimension model of selfhood. A simple independent vs interdependent contrast does not fit global variation.
numbers: Study 1: N = 2,924 students, 16 nations. Study 2: N = 7,279 adults, 55 cultural groups, 33 nations.
quote: a simple contrast between independence and interdependence does not adequately capture the diverse models of selfhood
limits: Abstract only. Says the one-axis social orientation construct is too coarse, which is a boundary on the whole theory.
agent_relevance: One-axis 'independent vs interdependent' labels hide many dimensions. Do not reduce a case to one axis.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi & Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psychological Review 108(2):291-310
finding: Founding statement. East Asians are holistic (whole field, causality in the field, little use of categories and formal logic, dialectical reasoning). Westerners are analytic (object and category, rules, formal logic). The authors speculate that the origin is in different social systems.
numbers: Review, no single effect size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Group-level claim, mostly East Asian vs Western student samples.
agent_relevance: This is the source of the 'framings' the schema could borrow (context-first vs object-first) but as problem-class tools, not as identity.

source: Masuda & Nisbett (2001) Attending holistically versus analytically. JPSP 81(5):922-934
finding: Japanese and Americans watched underwater animated vignettes (Study 1) and wildlife photos (Study 2). Japanese made more statements about context and relations, and recognised old objects better in their original setting than in a new one. The setting change mattered little for Americans.
numbers: Two studies; sample sizes and effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Student samples, two countries. A single task paradigm, so no individual-level structure was tested.
agent_relevance: Classic paradigm that Sabir et al. 2025 and Hu et al. 2026 adapt to models (object vs background in descriptions).

source: Uskul, Kitayama & Nisbett (2008) Ecocultural basis of cognition: farmers and fishermen are more holistic than herders. PNAS 105(25):8552-8556
finding: Three communities in Turkey's eastern Black Sea region, same nation, ethnicity and language. Farming and fishing communities (interdependent) were more holistic in attention, categorisation and reasoning than herding communities.
numbers: Sample sizes and statistics not read. An erratum exists (PNAS 105(33):12094).
limits: Abstract only. Group comparison. Used by the theory to rule out language and genes.
agent_relevance: Shows that economy or livelihood moves the group mean; no claim about individual prediction.

source: Kitayama, Ishii, Imada, Takemura & Ramaswamy (2006) Voluntary settlement and the spirit of independence: Japan's northern frontier. JPSP 91(3):369-384
finding: Hokkaido residents (descendants of 1870s settlers) were nearly as likely as European Americans to link happiness with personal achievement (Study 1), show personal dissonance (Study 2) and commit the dispositional bias in attribution (Study 3). Non-Hokkaido Japanese did not.
numbers: Three studies; sample sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Group-level, one region.
agent_relevance: Group style can shift with history inside one nation; one more reason a country label is a poor guide to a person.

source: Kitayama, Park, Sevincer, Karasawa & Uskul (2009) A cultural task analysis of implicit independence. JPSP 97(2):236-255
finding: Implicit markers of independence (focused attention, disengaging emotions, achievement-linked happiness, inflated symbolic self) were higher in North Americans than in British and Germans, with the two Western European groups not different. Japanese were less independent on all implicit markers. The explicit self-belief measure showed an anomalous pattern.
numbers: Sample sizes and effect sizes not read.
quote: An explicit self-belief measure of independence and interdependence showed an anomalous pattern.
limits: Abstract only. Implicit-vs-explicit gap supports the view that self-report and behaviour measures do not line up.
agent_relevance: Self-description and behaviour diverge in people; in models too (see Jin et al. 2023, a17 and a18).

source: Choi, Koo & Choi (2007) Individual differences in analytic versus holistic thinking. Pers Soc Psychol Bull 33(5):691-705
finding: Built the 24-item Analysis-Holism Scale (AHS) with six studies. Koreans scored higher than Americans; Korean students of Oriental medicine higher than non-Oriental majors. High AHS scores predicted the holistic pattern in a categorisation task and a causal reasoning task.
numbers: 24 items, 6 studies (factor analyses, convergent validity, known groups, two predictive studies). Effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. This is an earlier claim of individual-level validity for self-report; Na et al. (2010) later found weak coherence across a larger battery. Note: the two are not strictly contradictory (one scale vs 10 measures).
agent_relevance: The AHS is the instrument Jin et al. 2023 gave to ChatGPT. Its individual-level validity for people is itself contested.

source: Talhelm, Zhang, Oishi, Shimin, Duan, Lan & Kitayama (2014) Large-scale psychological differences within China explained by rice versus wheat agriculture. Science 344:603-608
finding: Rice-growing southern China was more interdependent and holistic than wheat-growing northern China. Neighbouring counties on the rice-wheat border showed differences just as large. Modernization and pathogen-prevalence accounts did not fit.
numbers: N = 1,162 Han Chinese in six sites (abstract).
limits: Abstract only. Group-level, regional means. Replication status not checked in this session (other agents cover it).
agent_relevance: Another group-level causal story. Same caution for single cases.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu & Cui (2023) The cultural psychology of large language models: is ChatGPT a holistic or analytic thinker? arXiv:2308.14242
finding: Gave GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 four human scales: Analysis-Holism Scale (AHS), Triadic Categorization Task (TCT), Dialectical Self Scale (DSS), Self-construal Scale (SCS). Both models scored more holistic than the human norm on the cognitive-process measures (AHS, TCT).
numbers: 10 repetitions per condition. AHS: GPT-3.5 M = 5.35 (SD 0.11), GPT-4 M = 5.01 (SD 0.10), human norm M = 4.87 (SD 0.49, N = 702), p < .001 both. TCT proportion relational: GPT-3.5 0.87, GPT-4 0.85, above most Chinese provinces in the cited data.
quote: ChatGPT consistently tends towards Eastern holistic thinking
limits: Only ChatGPT; N = 10 runs per condition (not independent people); human norms from other studies; the text says the baseline is temperature 1 in Table 1 but temperature 0 in Methods (inconsistent). A preprint with the TCT norm missing.
agent_relevance: They treat a group-validated scale as a trait test for one model. A model run is not a person drawn from a population, so the individual-level validity problem (a01) applies fully.

source: Jin et al. (2023) arXiv:2308.14242, value scales
finding: On value and self-construal scales the picture was mixed. GPT-3.5 sat above the human norm on both independent and interdependent self-construal. GPT-4 was above norm on independent, near norm on interdependent, and at norm on the Dialectical Self Scale.
limits: GPT-3.5 gave 'strongly agree' to almost everything (acquiescence), so scale scores are inflated for both subscales. Tiny SDs across runs show the model is near-deterministic, unlike human spread.
agent_relevance: The measured 'orientation' flips with the instrument (holistic on cognition scales, no lean on value scales): the two domains do not line up inside the model, echoing Na et al.'s weak cross-measure links in people.

source: Jin et al. (2023) arXiv:2308.14242, robustness
finding: Design: 14 conditions per model (temperature 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, plus three reworded prompt sets), 10 repetitions each. Authors say the findings held across them.
numbers: (1+3+3) x 2 models = 14 conditions x 10 repetitions. Robustness shown in a figure only; no table of numbers read.
limits: Claim of robustness rests on a figure. At temperature 0 the SD is zero by construction, so repetition adds nothing there.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run noise is small; the real unknown is variation across prompts and instruments, which this study tests only lightly.

source: Sabir, Gasper, Loem & Sharma (2025) Contrasting cognitive styles in vision-language models: holistic attention in Japanese versus analytical focus in English. arXiv:2507.00700
finding: Captions of 5K filtered COCO images were generated in English and Japanese by several models, then GPT-4o judged each caption as holistic (background first) or analytic (object first). Japanese output was more holistic than English output for GPT-4o, but the effect was small on COCO.
numbers: 5K COCO: GPT-4o 5-shot 19.22% holistic; GPT-4o-JP 23.64%; balanced 6-shot 19.80% vs 28.64%. Gemma-3-12B 14.16%; Gemma-3-27B-JP 13.50% (5-shot) and 21.14% (6-shot balanced). VILA-JP-14B (Japanese-trained) 13.88% and 16.90%.
limits: The judge is GPT-4o with few-shot prompts, so the label can be biased by the judge and the shot choice (5-shot vs 6-shot changes Gemma-JP from 13.50% to 21.14%). The Japanese-trained VILA-JP was less holistic than GPT-4o-JP.
agent_relevance: The 'cultural' effect in a model depends on the judge, the prompt, and the image set. It is a distribution shift, not a stable trait.

source: Sabir et al. (2025) arXiv:2507.00700, dataset and language effects
finding: On Japanese cultural images the holistic share rose strongly. Translating captions moved the labels by about 13 points on average, and back-translation partly reversed it. So output language and image content both shift the label.
numbers: GPT-4o-JP 6-shot: 26.10% holistic (COCO 1K) to 73.37% (1K Japanese photo set); HERON-Bench 53.49%; JA-VLM 61.90%. Plain GPT-4o on the 1K Japanese set: 59.10% (5-shot). English vs Japanese-original COCO captions (5K, 6-shot): 12.34% vs 27.48% holistic; machine-translated Japanese 27.54%. Human check, 200 images: VILA-JP 15.33% and GPT-4o-JP 17.75% holistic vs GPT-4o judge 19.50% and 29.00%.
limits: Human judges (3 native Japanese speakers) disagree with GPT-4o on size (17.75% vs 29.00% for GPT-4o-JP). Plain English GPT-4o also reaches 59.10% on Japanese images, so image content, not model culture, drives much of it.
agent_relevance: Task content changes the 'style' more than model identity. Supports: choose framing by problem class, not by a cultural label.

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung & Peng (2026) Beyond instrumental and substitutive paradigms: Machine culture as an emergent phenomenon in LLMs. arXiv:2601.17096
finding: 2 (model origin: US GPT-4o/DALL-E 3 vs Chinese ERNIE 4.5/iRAG-1.0) x 2 (prompt language: English vs Chinese) design over eight tasks (landscape drawing, scene description, attribution, triad categorisation, success/failure images, face-smile choice, ideal affect, ideal state). Model origin did not predict human-like cultural patterns; several effects ran opposite to the human direction.
numbers: Relational-minus-categorical score (Task 4): US model M = 8.10 (SD 1.44) vs Chinese model M = 6.04 (SD 1.54), t = -13.81, d = 1.38 (opposite to human East-Asian relational preference). Landscape object count: US 11.53 vs Chinese 8.10, d = 1.01. Scene description object count: Chinese 12.31 vs US 8.66, d = 2.42. Collective attribution: Chinese 3.17 vs US 2.81, d = 1.14; individual attribution: Chinese 4.75 vs US 4.67, d = 0.27 (both higher in the Chinese model).
limits: Only two models; text analysis done by DeepSeek-V3 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet; one prompt per task set (details not fully read). Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: The model-level direction flips from task to task. The two cognitive tasks (landscape generation vs scene description) disagree inside the same model, the same lack of cross-measure coherence Na et al. report for people.

source: Hu et al. (2026) arXiv:2601.17096, language priming results
finding: Prompt language did not switch cultural thinking in a stable way. Chinese prompts gave more landscape objects but English prompts gave more objects in scene descriptions (reversal). In triad categorisation there was no language effect overall, but the Chinese model scored lower on relational pairing in Chinese than in English.
numbers: Landscape objects: Chinese prompt M = 10.71 vs English M = 8.91, d = 0.49. Horizon height: no difference (523.20 vs 530.06, p = .096, d = 0.17). Scene object count: English 10.90 vs Chinese 10.06, t = -3.60, p < .001, d = 0.36. R-C score: Chinese 7.10 vs English 7.04, p = .741, d = 0.03. Chinese model R-C: Chinese 5.30 vs English 6.78, t = -7.74. Model x language interaction on attribution: F(1,396) = 18.21, p < .001.
limits: Preprint; effect sizes from many generations of one prompt, so p-values reflect run noise, not population sampling.
agent_relevance: A language or persona cue gives task-specific, sometimes reversed effects. Do not build a persona router on the assumption that it moves thinking style in the human direction.

source: Hu et al. (2026) arXiv:2601.17096, affect results and RLHF explanation
finding: Image generation followed stereotypes (US model more high-arousal positive, Chinese model more low-arousal positive), but text tasks did not. Authors name a 'Service Persona Camouflage': RLHF flattens affect answers to a positive, low-variance helper persona.
numbers: Success images: HAP US 113 vs Chinese 79, chi2 = 28.36, p < .001; LAP Chinese 41 vs US 2, chi2 = 40.91. Big smiles seen as Ideal: Chinese model 0.78 vs US 0.60, t(1553.54) = 8.10, d = 0.40, opposite to the human US preference.
limits: Mechanisms (curse of recursion, alignment tax) are the authors' interpretation, not tested. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Alignment training may remove between-group variation in stated style, which also means a group-level cultural finding is a poor guide to a tuned model.

source: Tao, Viberg, Baker & Kizilcec (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of large language models. arXiv:2311.14096 (PNAS Nexus)
finding: Five GPT models answered ten World Values Survey items, each in ten prompt variants, mapped on the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map. All models resemble English-speaking and Protestant European countries. 'Cultural prompting' (answer as a person from country X) moves the output nearer to the target country in most but not all countries.
numbers: GPT-4o nearest to Finland (distance 0.20), Andorra (0.21), Netherlands (0.45); farthest from Jordan (4.10), Libya (4.00), Ghana (3.95). Cultural prompting cuts mean distance from 2.42 to 1.57 (GPT-4o), 2.71 to 1.77 (GPT-4-turbo), 2.69 to 1.65 (GPT-4), 2.39 to 2.11 (GPT-3), 3.35 to 2.83 (GPT-3.5-turbo), all P < 0.001. It improves alignment for 71.0% (GPT-4o), 81.3% (GPT-4-turbo), 77.6% (GPT-4), 72.6% (GPT-3.5-turbo), 80.4% (GPT-3) of countries.
limits: Compares with country means from survey data, so it is a group-level test, not individual. Roughly 20-29% of countries get worse. Only ten survey items.
agent_relevance: A cultural persona can pull the mean toward a group average but not for every group. Matches 'group effect, not single case'.

source: AlKhamissi, ElNokrashy, AlKhamissi & Diab (2024) Investigating cultural alignment of large language models. arXiv:2402.13231
finding: Simulated a survey from Egypt and the US by prompting LLMs with the personas of real respondents. Alignment is higher when the prompt language is the dominant language of the culture and when pretraining mixes that language. Misalignment is larger for underrepresented personas and culturally sensitive topics. A prompting method called anthropological prompting improved alignment.
numbers: Abstract-level claims and section headings read; per-model soft/hard alignment scores not extracted in this session.
limits: Only skimmed the PDF text; no exact figures recorded. Two countries.
agent_relevance: Persona-conditioned prediction of individual respondents is the exact use case where group-level cultural knowledge is tested at the individual level; it works only partly.

source: Hu & Collier (2024) Quantifying the persona effect in LLM simulations. arXiv:2402.10811 (ACL 2024)
finding: Persona variables (demographic, social, behavioural) explain little of individual annotation variance. Prompting an LLM with a persona gives small but significant gains, largest when annotators disagree only a little. A 70B model with persona prompting reaches 81% of what a regression trained on ground truth can do, but only where persona variables carry signal.
numbers: Persona variables account for <10% of variance in annotations in many subjective NLP datasets (linear regression R2). 81% of the achievable variance is captured by the 70B model in zero-shot persona prompting.
quote: persona variables account for <10% variance in annotations in existing subjective NLP datasets
limits: Annotation tasks, not cognitive style tasks. Authors' own wording.
agent_relevance: Direct parallel: group membership explains a small share of individual variance, so persona prompts give limited gain.

source: Park, Zou, Kamphorst et al. (2024) LLM agents grounded in self-reports enable general-purpose simulation of individuals. arXiv:2411.10109
finding: 1,052 Americans were interviewed for two hours; agents built from the interview or surveys predicted each person's own General Social Survey answers far better than agents built from demographics alone. Individual data beats group labels.
numbers: GSS normalized accuracy (agent accuracy / person's own two-week retest): interview 0.83 (raw 65.67% / self-consistency 79.53%), survey 0.82, survey+interview 0.86, demographics-only 0.74, persona-only 0.71. ANOVA F(4, 5255) = 577.83, p < .001. Big Five: interview agents r = 0.78, normalized 0.80; demographic 0.61; persona 0.75; survey-only 0.65.
limits: US sample only. Demographic agents still reach 0.74, so group labels are not useless for attitudes. Big Five prediction from surveys was no better than baselines.
agent_relevance: Best-case evidence for individual-level prediction: it needs person-specific data. A group label alone leaves a gap of about 10 points (0.74 vs 0.83-0.86).

source: Wang, Morgenstern & Dickerson (2025) LLMs that replace human participants can harmfully misportray and flatten identity groups. arXiv:2402.01908 (Nature Machine Intelligence)
finding: Four LLMs prompted with identity labels give group portraits that look like out-group views (misportrayal) and are less varied than real in-group answers (flattening). Studies used 3,200 human participants across 16 identities.
numbers: 3,200 participants, 16 demographic identities, 4 LLMs. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 covered only about 3 of the 5 multiple-choice options across 100 responses per scenario.
limits: Read abstract and diversity section only; identity prompting can also essentialize identities. Diversity matches human only at temperatures that make the text incoherent.
agent_relevance: Group prompts produce one flat typical case; real group members vary. A scaffold should not depend on an assumed typical style.

source: Shweder (1973) The between and within of cross-cultural research. Ethos 1:531-545, as cited by Varnum et al. (2010)
finding: The older methodological point behind Na et al.: between-group and within-group structure can differ. Varnum et al. cite it for the claim that large group differences can sit beside very weak within-group differences on the same measures.
numbers: None. Original paper not opened; known only through the citation in Varnum et al.
limits: Cited at second hand.
agent_relevance: The statistical point (ecological structure is not individual structure) is old and general; it applies to any group-level finding we might use.
